q: Chronic diarrhoea lasts longer than how many weeks?
why: Acute is under 14 days (mostly infective), persistent 14–30 days, chronic over 4 weeks, which shifts the differential towards IBD, coeliac, malabsorption and cancer.

q: Total body water in a 70 kg man is about how many litres?
why: Water is about 60% of body weight in an adult man (70 × 0.6 ≈ 42 L): two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular.

q: FEV1/FVC ratio below which airflow obstruction is diagnosed?
why: A ratio under 0.7 means FEV1 is disproportionately reduced, the hallmark of airflow obstruction.

q: LTOT is offered if PaO₂ is below what (kPa) on two readings?
why: Long-term oxygen improves survival in COPD only if PaO₂ is below 7.3 kPa (or 7.3–8 with polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension or oedema), measured twice 3 weeks apart when stable.

q: Target oxygen saturations in a COPD patient at risk of CO₂ retention?
why: A lower target of 88–92% avoids worsening hypercapnia in patients who retain CO₂.

q: Prednisolone dose for a COPD exacerbation?
why: 30 mg for 5 days speeds recovery and reduces treatment failure in COPD exacerbations; longer courses add side effects without benefit.

q: Normal adult tidal volume?
why: A normal breath is about 500 mL (roughly 7 mL/kg), of which about 150 mL stays in the dead space.

q: Anatomical dead space in an adult?
why: About 150 mL (roughly 2 mL/kg) fills the conducting airways and never reaches the alveoli.

q: Normal anion gap (with K⁺)?
why: Anion gap = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normally about 10–18 mmol/L; a high gap means unmeasured acids such as ketones or lactate.

q: Calf circumference difference that scores on the Wells DVT score?
why: A calf swollen 3 cm or more than the other side (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity) scores a point on the Wells DVT score.

q: Pleural effusion pH below which a chest drain is needed (empyema)?
why: A pleural pH below 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion means an empyema is developing and needs a chest drain.

q: Light's criteria: pleural/serum protein ratio above which it's an exudate?
why: If the pleural:serum protein ratio is above 0.5, the effusion is an exudate (leaky capillaries or inflammation), not a transudate.

q: Steady state is reached after about how many half-lives?
why: Each half-life closes half the remaining gap to steady state, so after 4–5 half-lives you're at about 94–97% (the same applies to elimination).

q: Normal PR interval (seconds)?
why: The PR interval of 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares) reflects AV nodal delay; longer is heart block, shorter suggests pre-excitation.

q: QRS duration above which it's broad?
why: A QRS of 0.12 s (3 small squares) or more means slow ventricular conduction (bundle branch block, ventricular rhythm or hyperkalaemia).

q: Upper limit of normal QTc in men?
why: QTc above 440 ms in men (460 in women) is prolonged and raises the risk of torsades de pointes.

q: 1st-degree heart block: PR interval above?
why: First-degree heart block is a PR over 200 ms (one large square) with every P wave conducted.

q: Age by which a child should walk (upper limit)?
why: Most children walk by 12–15 months; not walking by 18 months needs assessment (check CK in boys for Duchenne).

q: Age by which a baby should sit unsupported (upper limit)?
why: Most babies sit unsupported by 6–8 months as trunk control develops from the head down; not sitting by 9 months is a red flag for referral.

q: Age of the first social smile?
why: The first social smile appears at about 6 weeks; no smile by 8 weeks warrants review.

q: Folic acid dose for a woman at high risk of a neural tube defect?
why: High-risk women (previous NTD, diabetes, epilepsy drugs, BMI ≥30) take 5 mg daily rather than 400 μg, from before conception to 12 weeks.

q: Normal GFR?
why: Normal GFR is about 125 mL/min (180 L/day), so most filtrate is reabsorbed to leave about 1.5 L of urine.

q: Ureteric stone size most likely to pass spontaneously?
why: Stones under 5 mm usually pass on their own; larger ones are less likely to and may need intervention.

q: BMI defining obesity class III?
why: BMI 30–34.9 is class I, 35–39.9 class II and 40 or above class III (severe) obesity.

q: BMI threshold for bariatric surgery with significant comorbidity?
why: Bariatric surgery is considered at BMI 35 or above with significant comorbidity (40 without), after non-surgical measures.

q: QRISK3 above which atorvastatin 20 mg is offered for primary prevention?
why: NICE offers atorvastatin 20 mg when 10-year cardiovascular risk is 10% or more.

q: Atorvastatin dose for secondary prevention?
why: High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg is used for secondary prevention after cardiovascular events to lower LDL as much as possible.

q: Dating scan window (weeks)?
why: The dating scan is done at 10+0 to 13+6 weeks, when crown–rump length is most accurate and nuchal translucency can be measured.

q: Gestational diabetes thresholds on a 75 g OGTT (fasting, 2 h)?
why: NICE diagnoses gestational diabetes with fasting glucose of 5.6 or more, or a 2-hour level of 7.8 or more, on a 75 g OGTT.

q: Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention starts at how many weeks?
why: Low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia in high-risk women by improving placental development.

q: Hb threshold for anaemia in the 1st trimester?
why: Haemoglobin naturally falls in pregnancy as plasma expands, so the anaemia cut-off is lower than usual: below 110 g/L in the first trimester.

q: PPH is blood loss over how many mL?
why: PPH is blood loss over 500 mL after a vaginal birth; over 1000 mL is major.

q: Legal time limit for most terminations under the Abortion Act?
why: Most terminations are legal up to 24 weeks; beyond that, only for serious risk to the woman or serious fetal anomaly.

q: Oseltamivir works best when started within how many hours?
why: Oseltamivir stops viral release, so it helps most within 48 hours, when the virus is still replicating rapidly.

q: Dexamethasone dose for COVID-19 needing oxygen?
why: RECOVERY used dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days in hospitalised patients needing oxygen.

q: Continue an antidepressant for at least how long after remission?
why: Continuing an antidepressant for at least 6 months after remission halves the risk of relapse.

q: Target serum urate on allopurinol?
why: Below 0.36 mmol/L urate dissolves existing crystals and prevents new ones (below 0.30 if tophi or frequent flares).

q: Corrected calcium formula: add 0.02 × (40 − albumin). Normal range?
why: Normal adjusted calcium is about 2.2–2.6 mmol/L; correct for albumin because half of calcium is protein-bound.

q: IV/IM hydrocortisone dose in adrenal crisis?
why: Adrenal crisis needs 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM immediately, then fluids and further doses.

q: CURB-65: urea above?
why: Urea above 7 mmol/L reflects dehydration and sepsis severity and scores a point.

q: CURB-65: respiratory rate of at least?
why: A respiratory rate of 30 or more scores a point, reflecting respiratory compromise.

q: Length of standard TB treatment (months)?
why: Standard TB treatment is 6 months: 2 months of four drugs (RIPE), then 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid.

q: Fluid bolus volume for resuscitation (crystalloid)?
why: A 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes, then reassess, avoids fluid overload while restoring perfusion.

q: Daily maintenance water for adults?
why: Adults need about 25–30 mL/kg/day of water, plus about 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride.

q: Max IV potassium rate through a peripheral line?
why: Faster potassium through a peripheral line risks arrhythmias and vein irritation, so 10 mmol/h is the usual maximum.

q: AKI (KDIGO): rise in creatinine within 48 h?
why: A creatinine rise of 26 μmol/L or more within 48 hours (or 1.5× baseline within 7 days) defines AKI.

q: AKI: urine output below what for 6 hours?
why: Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 hours defines AKI.

q: Potassium at which emergency treatment is needed?
why: Potassium of 6.5 or above (or any level with ECG changes) needs emergency treatment: calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol.

q: CKD: albuminuria defined by urine ACR of at least?
why: An ACR of 3 mg/mmol or more means albuminuria, which marks kidney damage and raises cardiovascular risk.

q: Target INR for VTE or AF on warfarin?
why: For VTE and AF the INR target is 2.5 (range 2–3), balancing clot prevention against bleeding; mechanical valves need higher.

q: HbA1c diagnostic of diabetes?
why: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above diagnoses diabetes, reflecting average glucose over about 3 months.

q: Fasting glucose diagnostic of diabetes?
why: Fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more diagnoses diabetes; 6.1–6.9 is impaired fasting glucose.

q: Random glucose diagnostic of diabetes (with symptoms)?
why: A random glucose of 11.1 or more with symptoms diagnoses diabetes.

q: Hypoglycaemia is glucose below?
why: Glucose below 4 mmol/L is hypoglycaemia ("four is the floor"), when symptoms start and treatment is needed.

q: HHS: osmolality above?
why: HHS is defined by marked hyperglycaemia, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and dehydration without significant ketosis.

q: Metformin is stopped when eGFR falls below?
why: Metformin is stopped when eGFR falls below 30 because it builds up and raises the risk of lactic acidosis (review the dose below 45).

q: IM adrenaline dose in adult anaphylaxis?
why: 500 μg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM is the adult dose: enough to reverse vasodilation and airway swelling quickly.

q: Repeat IM adrenaline after how many minutes?
why: Repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there's no improvement; two doses without response is refractory anaphylaxis.

q: Lactate above which septic shock is defined (with vasopressors)?
why: Septic shock is sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids.

q: MAP target in septic shock on noradrenaline?
why: A MAP of 65 mmHg keeps organs perfused while avoiding excessive vasopressor use.

q: Window for testicular salvage in torsion?
why: Testicular salvage rates are high within 6 hours of torsion and fall sharply after, so surgery shouldn't wait for scans.

q: Normal intraocular pressure?
why: Normal pressure is 10–21 mmHg; higher pressure is the main modifiable risk factor for glaucomatous nerve damage.

q: Severe aortic stenosis: mean gradient above?
why: A mean gradient above 40 mmHg across the valve marks severe aortic stenosis, a trigger for valve replacement if symptomatic.

q: Severe aortic stenosis: valve area below?
why: A valve area below 1.0 cm² (normal is 3–4) defines severe aortic stenosis.

q: Number of blood culture sets in suspected endocarditis?
why: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites and times maximise the chance of catching continuous bacteraemia and spotting contaminants.

q: Parasitaemia above which UK guidance calls falciparum malaria severe?
why: UK guidance treats falciparum malaria as severe if parasitaemia is above 2% (or with severe features), needing IV artesunate.

q: SDG target for maternal mortality ratio (per 100,000 live births)?
why: The Sustainable Development Goals aim to cut the global maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 live births by 2030.

q: Gestation below which magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection?
why: Magnesium sulfate given before birth under 30 weeks protects the fetal brain and reduces cerebral palsy.

q: Extremely preterm means born before how many weeks?
why: Babies born before 28 weeks are extremely preterm, with the highest risks of death and disability.

q: TEN-4: any bruise in an infant younger than how many months is suspicious?
why: TEN-4-FACESp flags bruising on torso, ears or neck in under-4s, and any bruise in an infant under 4 months.

q: FeNO level diagnostic of asthma in adults?
why: FeNO of 50 ppb or more in adults supports asthma by showing eosinophilic airway inflammation.

q: Bronchodilator reversibility: FEV1 rise of at least?
why: An FEV1 rise of 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator supports asthma.

q: Peak flow variability that supports asthma?
why: Peak flow variability above 20% over 2 weeks supports asthma.

q: Acute severe asthma: PEF as % best?
why: PEF 33–50% of best or predicted defines acute severe asthma; below 33% is life-threatening.

q: Life-threatening asthma: sats below?
why: Sats below 92% in acute asthma are a life-threatening feature, so check a blood gas.

q: IV magnesium sulfate dose in acute severe asthma?
why: A single 2 g IV dose of magnesium sulfate over 20 minutes relaxes bronchial smooth muscle in acute severe asthma.

q: Cardiothoracic ratio above which the heart is enlarged (PA film)?
why: On a PA film, a heart wider than half the chest width (CTR above 0.5) means cardiomegaly; AP films exaggerate heart size.

q: Neutropenic sepsis: neutrophils below?
why: Neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L with fever or sepsis means neutropenic sepsis, needing IV antibiotics within an hour.

q: AIDS-defining CD4 count?
why: A CD4 count below 200 cells/μL defines AIDS and greatly raises the risk of opportunistic infections such as PCP.

q: PEP must start within how many hours?
why: PEP must start within 72 hours, ideally within 24, to stop the virus establishing infection.

q: Fixed-rate insulin dose in DKA?
why: A fixed-rate infusion of 0.1 units/kg/h switches off ketone production regardless of glucose level.

q: Add 10% glucose in DKA when glucose falls below?
why: Once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, 10% glucose is added so insulin can continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycaemia.

q: DKA: ketones of at least?
why: Ketones of 3.0 mmol/L or more (with acidosis and hyperglycaemia or known diabetes) define DKA.

q: DKA resolution: ketones below and pH above?
why: DKA has resolved when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and pH above 7.3; then switch to subcutaneous insulin.

q: IBS: symptoms for how many months before diagnosis?
why: Rome IV requires symptoms for the last 3 months with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis.

q: Starting feed rate in high refeeding risk?
why: High-risk patients start at 5–10 kcal/kg/day and increase slowly to avoid refeeding syndrome.

q: Upper normal diameters: small bowel / colon / caecum?
why: The 3/6/9 rule: small bowel above 3 cm, colon above 6 cm and caecum above 9 cm are dilated.

q: Severe OSA: AHI above?
why: AHI counts apnoeas and hypopnoeas per hour: 5–14 mild, 15–30 moderate, above 30 severe.

q: Epworth score above which sleepiness is excessive?
why: An Epworth score above 10 (out of 24) means excessive daytime sleepiness.

q: NIV criteria in COPD: pH and PaCO₂?
why: NIV is indicated for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH below 7.35 and PaCO₂ above 6.5 kPa despite optimal treatment.

q: ACE-III total score?
why: ACE-III is scored out of 100 across five cognitive domains.

q: ACE-III cut-off with high specificity for dementia?
why: A score of 82 or below has high specificity for dementia; 88 is the more sensitive cut-off.

q: Thrombolysis window in ischaemic stroke?
why: Alteplase is licensed within 4.5 hours of stroke onset; benefit falls and bleeding risk rises after that.

q: AAA referral threshold?
why: AAAs of 5.5 cm or more have a rupture risk that outweighs surgical risk, so they're referred within 2 weeks.

q: Age of men offered one-off AAA screening?
why: Men are offered a one-off AAA screening ultrasound in the year they turn 65.

q: ABPI below which PAD is diagnosed?
why: An ABPI below 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease.

q: ABPI at or above which full compression is safe?
why: Full compression is generally safe when ABPI is 0.8 or above; below that, arterial supply may be too poor.

q: ABPI suggesting calcified incompressible arteries?
why: An ABPI above 1.3 suggests calcified, incompressible arteries (diabetes, CKD) and is unreliable.

q: Compartment syndrome: ΔP (diastolic − compartment) below?
why: A perfusion pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg indicates compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy.

q: Hip fracture surgery should happen within?
why: Surgery within 36 hours reduces mortality and complications after hip fracture.

q: NT-proBNP above which echo is needed within 2 weeks?
why: NT-proBNP above 2000 ng/L means a high chance of heart failure, so echo and specialist review within 2 weeks.

q: HFrEF: LVEF at or below?
why: An LVEF of 40% or below defines HFrEF.

q: ICD for primary prevention if LVEF at or below?
why: An ICD is considered for primary prevention when LVEF is 35% or below despite optimal treatment, because the risk of sudden arrhythmic death is high.

q: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy if hCG is below?
why: Methotrexate works best for small, unruptured ectopics with hCG below 1500 IU/L, no heartbeat and little pain.

q: Average age of menopause in the UK?
why: The average age of menopause in the UK is 51.

q: Premature ovarian insufficiency: before what age?
why: Menopause before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency.

q: Down's screening "higher chance" cut-off?
why: A combined test result of 1 in 150 or higher counts as a "higher chance", leading to the offer of NIPT or invasive testing.

q: Wells PE score above which CTPA is first?
why: A Wells score over 4 means PE is likely, so request CTPA straight away.

q: Anticoagulation for a provoked PE?
why: Three months of anticoagulation is usually enough for a PE with a clear temporary trigger.

q: Pulmonary hypertension: mean PA pressure above (2022)?
why: The 2022 ESC/ERS definition lowered the threshold to mean PA pressure above 20 mmHg at rest.

q: Normal PaCO₂ range (kPa)?
why: Normal PaCO₂ is 4.7–6.0 kPa; above that is hypercapnia (respiratory acidosis if acute).

q: Normal PaO₂ on air (kPa)?
why: Normal PaO₂ breathing air is about 10–13 kPa.

q: Respiratory failure: PaO₂ below (kPa)?
why: Respiratory failure is PaO₂ below 8 kPa; it's type 2 if PaCO₂ is above 6.

q: Primary PCI if it can be delivered within how many minutes?
why: Primary PCI is preferred if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given; otherwise give fibrinolysis.

q: Aspirin loading dose in ACS?
why: 300 mg aspirin rapidly inhibits platelet thromboxane in acute coronary syndromes.

q: Length of dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS?
why: Dual antiplatelet therapy usually lasts 12 months after ACS.

q: Driving after successful PCI for ACS (LVEF >40%)?
why: After successful PCI with LVEF above 40%, car drivers can usually resume after 1 week (4 weeks otherwise).

q: Vertebral level of the transpyloric plane?
why: Halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis, it crosses the pylorus, pancreatic neck, renal hila and SMA origin.

q: Vertebral level of the umbilicus (in a slim adult)?
why: The umbilicus lies at about the L3/4 disc, in the T10 dermatome; it moves down with obesity and age.

q: Approximate length of the adult ureter?
why: About 25 cm, half in the abdomen and half in the pelvis; it narrows at the PUJ, pelvic brim and VUJ.

q: Normal adult bladder capacity?
why: Roughly 400–600 mL; the first urge to void comes at about 150–300 mL.

q: Length of the female urethra?
why: Short and straight, so UTIs are commoner in women and catheterisation is easier.

q: Total length of the male urethra?
why: About 18–22 cm: prostatic (3–4 cm), membranous (1–2 cm) and spongy (~15 cm) parts.

q: Total degrees of midgut rotation around the SMA?
why: 90° while herniated and 180° on returning, all anticlockwise viewed from the front.

q: Week by which the herniated midgut has returned to the abdomen?
why: It herniates in week 6, rotates, and is back by the end of week 10.

q: Meckel's diverticulum lies about how far from the ileocaecal valve?
why: Rule of 2s: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 tissue types.

q: Number of tendons passing through the carpal tunnel?
why: Four FDS, four FDP and FPL, plus the median nerve.

q: Number of carpal bones in one wrist?
why: Proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

q: Number of phalanges in one hand?
why: Two in the thumb and three in each finger.

q: Gestation at which the uterine fundus reaches the umbilicus?
why: It reaches the symphysis at ~12 weeks and the xiphisternum at ~36 weeks.

q: Distance of the ureter from the cervix?
why: About 1.5–2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix, under the uterine artery, so it is at risk at hysterectomy.

q: Swelling within how many hours of a knee injury suggests haemarthrosis?
why: Rapid swelling means bleeding (ACL tear, fracture); a meniscal tear swells slowly over a day.

q: Age at which the triradiate cartilage of the acetabulum fuses?
why: The ilium, ischium and pubis meet here; it fuses after puberty.

q: Position of the great saphenous vein at the ankle relative to the medial malleolus?
why: A constant position, used for emergency venous cut-down even when veins are collapsed.

q: Tracheal rings covered by the thyroid isthmus?
why: The isthmus may need dividing at surgical tracheostomy.

q: Vertebral level of the hyoid bone?
why: The thyroid cartilage is at C4–5 and the cricoid at C6.

q: Vertebral level of the common carotid bifurcation?
why: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.

q: Distance above the clavicle at which the accessory nerve enters trapezius?
why: It crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is easily cut in lymph node biopsy.

q: Distance from the incisor teeth to the upper oesophageal sphincter?
why: Cricopharyngeus at C6; the lower sphincter is about 40 cm from the teeth.

q: Gestation from which surfactant is adequate in most fetuses?
why: Type II pneumocytes start making it at ~20–24 weeks; antenatal steroids are given if preterm birth is expected.

q: Age by which most alveoli have formed?
why: Most alveoli form after birth, through early childhood.

q: Number of pairs of spinal nerves?
why: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.

q: Vertebral level at which the adult spinal cord ends?
why: It ends at about L3 at birth; lumbar puncture is done at L3/4 or L4/5.

q: Vertebral level at which the dural sac ends?
why: The subarachnoid space with the cauda equina continues down to S2.

q: Vertebral level at which the arch of the aorta begins and ends?
why: At the sternal angle, which also marks the tracheal bifurcation and the 2nd costal cartilage.

q: Volume of rapidly collecting fluid that can cause cardiac tamponade?
why: The fibrous pericardium can't stretch quickly; a slow effusion can reach litres before tamponade.

q: Proportion of hearts that are right-dominant?
why: The RCA gives the posterior descending artery in most people; ~10% are left-dominant, the rest co-dominant.

q: Vertebral level of the aortic bifurcation?
why: About the level of the umbilicus and iliac crests.

q: Vertebral level of the coeliac trunk?
why: SMA at L1, renal arteries at L1/2, gonadal at L2, IMA at L3.

q: Vertebral level of the inferior mesenteric artery?
why: Coeliac T12, SMA L1, IMA L3.

q: Vertebral level at which the IVC passes through the diaphragm?
why: "I 8 10 eggs at 12": IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.

q: Vertebral level at which the IVC is formed?
why: The common iliac veins join behind the right common iliac artery.

q: Aortic diameter at which elective AAA repair is usually considered?
why: Above 5.5 cm the rupture risk outweighs the risk of surgery; 3.0 cm defines an aneurysm.

q: Approximate length of an adult kidney?
why: About 10–12 cm; a difference of more than 2 cm between sides is significant.

q: Number of deciduous teeth?
why: Five per quadrant: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars.

q: Age at which the first permanent molars erupt?
why: They erupt behind the deciduous teeth without replacing any.

q: Age at which the anterior fontanelle usually closes?
why: The posterior fontanelle closes at about 2–3 months.

q: Vertebral level of cricopharyngeus?
why: The pharynx becomes the oesophagus and the larynx becomes the trachea at C6.

q: Time within which a torted testis should be untwisted to give the best chance of saving it?
why: Salvage falls sharply after 6 hours; both testes are fixed at surgery.

q: Vertebral level of origin of the testicular arteries?
why: The testes develop on the posterior abdominal wall and bring their arteries with them.

q: How far below core temperature are the testes kept?
why: The pampiniform plexus and the dartos and cremaster muscles keep the testes cool for spermatogenesis.

q: Number of bones forming the orbit?
why: Frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, maxilla, zygomatic and palatine.

q: Proportion of salivary stones that form in the submandibular gland?
why: Its saliva is thicker and more alkaline, and its duct is long and runs uphill.

q: Number of circumvallate papillae on the tongue?
why: They form a V in front of the sulcus terminalis and carry many taste buds; supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

q: Roughly how much does the middle ear increase sound pressure?
why: The eardrum is about 17 times the area of the stapes footplate, and the ossicles add a small lever gain, matching air to fluid.

q: Length of the adult auditory tube?
why: In infants it is about half as long and more horizontal, so middle ear infections are commoner.

q: Typical subpubic angle in a female pelvis?
why: The male angle is narrower (about 50–60°), like the angle between two spread fingers versus thumb and index finger.

q: Normal pulmonary artery pressure?
why: The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, low-resistance system, so the right ventricle is thin-walled.

q: Thickness of the alveolar–capillary barrier?
why: Type I pneumocytes and capillary endothelium share a fused basement membrane, so gases diffuse quickly.

q: Approximate number of alveoli in adult lungs?
why: They give a gas exchange surface of about 70 m².

q: Normal carrying angle of the elbow?
why: The forearm angles outwards in extension, more in women; a changed angle after a supracondylar fracture gives cubitus varus or valgus.

q: Daily production of cerebrospinal fluid?
why: Made by the choroid plexus; the CSF is replaced about 3–4 times a day.

q: Total volume of cerebrospinal fluid at any time?
why: About 25 mL is in the ventricles and the rest in the subarachnoid space.

q: Normal CSF opening pressure at lumbar puncture (lying on the side)?
why: Raised in idiopathic intracranial hypertension, meningitis and venous sinus thrombosis.

q: How often are women screened with mammography in the NHS?
why: From 50 up to the 71st birthday; younger high-risk women may be screened yearly with MRI.

q: Typical length of the adult spleen?
why: "1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11": about 1 × 3 × 5 inches, 7 oz, lying under ribs 9–11; over ~13 cm on ultrasound is splenomegaly.

q: Vertebral level of the oesophageal hiatus?
why: "I 8 10 Eggs At 12": IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.

q: Portal hypertension is a hepatic venous pressure gradient above what?
why: At 10 mmHg or more it is clinically significant (varices can form); above 12 mmHg varices can bleed.

q: Distance of the saphenous opening below and lateral to the pubic tubercle?
why: The great saphenous vein passes through it to join the femoral vein (saphenofemoral junction).
